entries.clue: Some nonsense about racket that’s carved up fertile ground (5,5)

indicatorNotes.about: A story told about someone goes all the way round its subject, so one word here closes over another.
indicatorNotes.that’s carved up: A joint carved up leaves the table in pieces rather than whole, so these letters come apart and are re-laid in a new order.

blocks.note: blah is nonsense, empty talk, and it opens after its first three letters
the six letters of RACKET in a new order

annotation.surface: Gossip going round about a noisy swindle that has torn up good farmland.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nonsense' looks like the shuffling instruction and is not — it is a word in its own right, with the jumble dropped inside it. The soil meant is the belt that runs from Ukraine across southern Russia.
annotation.definitionFit: Black earth is chernozem, the deep dark humus-rich soil farmers prize above any other, so ground that is fertile is what the name says.

entries.clue: Macho guy promises on paper to be intellectual? (8)

blocks.note: a stud is a man who thinks himself irresistible
an IOU is a scribbled promise to pay, and here there are several

annotation.surface: A swaggering ladies' man whose written promises to pay hint at a bookish side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Promises' reads as a verb with the macho guy as its subject; it is a plural noun. IOUs are the standard way a setter buys the letters I, O and U.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone studious is given over to books and study, which is the adjective 'intellectual' applied to a person.

entries.clue: Detective receiving cut, having secured second data storage item (4)

indicatorNotes.receiving cut: A man who receives a cut comes away shorter than he went in, so the word loses its final letter.
indicatorNotes.having secured: To secure something is to hold it fast inside you, so what is named next is kept within these letters.

blocks.note: a dick is a detective in old crime slang, and the cut takes its last letter
s = second, the letter written after a count of them

annotation.surface: A detective on the take, pocketing his share after coming second in something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dick' for a detective is Chandler-era slang and still crossword currency. 'Cut' is the shortening here rather than a share of the money the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A disc is the round object data is written on to — a CD, or the platter spinning inside a hard drive.

entries.clue: Swiftness shown by father, out of delicacy (7)

indicatorNotes.out of: Taking one thing out of another leaves only what was not taken, so the priest's two letters go and the rest stands.

blocks.note: Fr is how a priest signs himself, short for Father
fragility is delicacy, and it is the word those two letters come out of

annotation.surface: A father moving quickly so as not to cause anyone embarrassment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of delicacy' reads as 'from tact' and is really an instruction to take letters away. Fr is the title printed in front of a Catholic priest's name.
annotation.definitionFit: Agility is quickness and lightness in moving, which is the noun 'swiftness' names.

entries.clue: Ready with odd book about origin of computer navigational aid (10)

indicatorNotes.about: What goes about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters assembled here open to admit the one that follows.

blocks.note: the ready is cash, and bread is slang for the same thing
the first letter of COMPUTER, which is where the word starts
rum means odd or peculiar, as in a rum do
b = book, the standard short form

annotation.surface: A peculiar book about where computers came from, and the cash to buy it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is money here — the ready, as in ready cash — and 'rum' is the old word for odd. The 'origin' wanted is simply the first letter of the word after it.
annotation.definitionFit: A breadcrumb is one of the markers Hansel dropped to find his way home, and websites now call their trail of links by the same name.

entries.clue: Spot that woman’s instrument (6)

blocks.note: a zit is a pimple, a spot on the skin
her is the possessive of 'that woman', as in that woman's coat

annotation.surface: Noticing the musical instrument a woman across the room is holding.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to point something out; 'spot' is the blemish instead. A zither is the flat stringed box played on a table, famous for the Third Man theme.
annotation.definitionFit: A zither is a stringed instrument, its strings stretched across a shallow soundbox and plucked, so the plain word covers it.

entries.clue: Prominent figure elevating new energy source (4)

indicatorNotes.elevating: To elevate is to carry upwards, and in a down clue letters carried upwards are read from the bottom of the column.

blocks.note: oil is an energy source, running up the column
n = new, the dictionary's short form

annotation.surface: A famous name lending weight to a new source of energy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elevating' works only because this is a down entry; the same three words across would need a different instruction. N for 'new' is one of the single letters worth learning cold.
annotation.definitionFit: A lion is a person of great note — a literary lion, a lion of the bar — which is the prominent-figure sense.

entries.clue: Heavy shoe enclosing sheer garments (8)

annotation.definitionNote: Garments is plural and clothing is a mass noun, but the two swap freely: a shop selling garments sells clothing.

indicatorNotes.enclosing: To enclose a thing is to shut it in on every side, so the shoe's letters close round what follows.

blocks.note: a clog is the wooden-soled shoe of the northern mill towns
sheer fabric is thin enough to see through

annotation.surface: A clumsy wooden shoe with something flimsy stuffed inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sheer' has several senses — utter, steep, vertical — and the fabric one is wanted. Clogs were the working footwear of the Lancashire mills, which is what makes them heavy.
annotation.definitionFit: Clothing is the collective word for the things people wear, which is what a pile of garments amounts to.

entries.clue: Dried food is submerged in water (6)

indicatorNotes.submerged in: Something submerged in water has the water closing over it on every side, so one word sits inside the other.

blocks.note: rain is water, and it parts in the middle
the word is used just as it stands

annotation.surface: A piece of dried food lying at the bottom of a glass of water.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a plain statement of fact, and that is the disguise: 'is' is not the verb joining two halves but two letters of the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A raisin is a grape dried in the sun and eaten as it is, so 'dried food' names it squarely.

entries.clue: One repeatedly interrupts Australian band, generating sharp response? (6)

indicatorNotes.repeatedly interrupts: To interrupt is to break in part-way through, and doing it repeatedly means breaking in at more than one place.

blocks.note: AC/DC, the Sydney rock band, written without its slash
the Roman numeral for one, breaking in after the first two letters
the same numeral a second time, which is what 'repeatedly' asks for
surface only — it says what sort of thing is being described, without adding letters

annotation.surface: A heckler breaking in on an Australian rock band and getting a tart answer back.
annotation.walkthrough: AC/DC are crossword regulars once you stop reading 'band' as a strip or a ring. 'Repeatedly' is doing real work: the same letter breaks in at two different points.
annotation.definitionFit: Something acidic tastes sharp on the tongue, and a remark can be acidic in that same biting way.

entries.clue: Disliking Liberal’s pledge in Government (8)

blocks.note: l = Liberal, the party letter beside a candidate's name
an oath is a solemn pledge
the word is used just as it stands
g = Government, the Whitehall short form

annotation.surface: A promise a Liberal made once his party was inside the Government.
annotation.walkthrough: Two of the four pieces are single letters off the political page, L for Liberal and G for Government. 'In' is simply itself, which is the easiest word in any clue to overlook.
annotation.definitionFit: To be loathing something is to be disliking it with disgust — the same act, several degrees stronger.

entries.clue: Scoundrel, after a lot of funny stuff, returned in charge of a sort of Government (10)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something stands behind it, so in an across entry the scoundrel's letters follow the ones he is put after.
indicatorNotes.a lot of: A lot of a thing is most of it and not all, so the word turns up without its final letter.
indicatorNotes.returned: Something returned comes back the way it went, so those letters are read from the end.

blocks.note: funny stuff is COMEDY, most of which is COMED, written back to front
a rat is a scoundrel, the sort who betrays his friends
i/c is in charge, as in the officer i/c stores

annotation.surface: A villain back from a comedy turn and now running some kind of government.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Scoundrel' is the only sign it belongs behind the rest rather than in front of it. 'In charge' is i/c, two letters off an army noticeboard.
annotation.definitionFit: Democratic describes whatever belongs to a democracy, which is one sort of government among monarchies and dictatorships.

entries.clue: Broadcast their carol, requiring no response? (10)

indicatorNotes.Broadcast: To broadcast seed is to fling it wide across a field, so the letters land in no particular order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: Someone's Christmas carol being put out on the radio.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is the farming sense, seed scattered by hand, rather than anything to do with radio. The question mark marks the definition as a description of a question rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: A rhetorical question is asked for effect with no answer expected, so it is precisely one requiring no response.

entries.clue: Stack building items, removing first and last (4)

indicatorNotes.removing first and last: Taking away the first and the last leaves everything between them, so both ends of the word drop off.

blocks.note: bricks are building items, and they give up their B and their S

annotation.surface: Piling up building materials, leaving out the first one and the last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stack' opens the clue looking like a verb of instruction and is in fact the definition, a noun. The shortest deletions are the hardest to see, because so little is left standing.
annotation.definitionFit: A rick is a stack of hay or straw built in the open field and thatched over against the rain.

entries.clue: Chapter not so much about French writer’s skill (10)

indicatorNotes.about: A book written about a man goes all round its subject, so these letters close over the name that follows.

blocks.note: c = chapter, the short form used in citations
less means not so much, and the word parts after its first two letters
Jules Verne, who wrote Around the World in Eighty Days

annotation.surface: A chapter that turns out not to be about a French novelist's craft after all.
annotation.walkthrough: Verne is the French writer setters reach for when they need those five letters. 'Not so much' is a comparative phrase pressed into service as a single word.
annotation.definitionFit: Cleverness is the knack of doing a thing well and ingeniously, the sense of skill that praises the trick rather than the training.

entries.clue: Exhausted soils within forest, say, providing shock (7)

indicatorNotes.Exhausted: Something exhausted has had the whole of its middle used up, so only the letters at each end are left standing.
indicatorNotes.within: What lies within a thing has that thing closed round it, so these letters go inside the others.

blocks.note: trees make a forest, and 'say' allows the loose equation
SOILS emptied of its middle leaves an S at each end

annotation.surface: Worn-out soil in the middle of a wood, and the alarm that causes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shock' reads as a jolt and is the hair sense, a shock of hair. 'Exhausted' is the emptying instruction: a word drained of everything but its two ends.
annotation.definitionFit: A shock is a thick unruly mass of hair, and tresses are the long hair that makes one, so both name what grows on a head.

entries.clue: Visitor having time off - she’s dodging husband’s suggestions? (7)

indicatorNotes.off: A day off is a day taken out of the week, so the letter named before it goes missing.
indicatorNotes.dodging: To dodge a thing is to keep clear of it altogether, so that letter never appears.

blocks.note: a guest is a visitor
t = time, the letter taken off
she's, the two words run together
h = husband, as on a form

annotation.surface: A visitor with an afternoon free, keeping out of the husband's way.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves lose one letter to a standard abbreviation, t for time and h for husband, and spotting the second is the work. The dash is punctuation, not instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A guess is a suggestion put forward without certainty, which is why the question mark softens the definition.

entries.clue: Mostly cancel insignificant investigation (8)

indicatorNotes.Mostly: Mostly means nearly all of it, so the word arrives without its final letter.

blocks.note: to scrub a plan is to cancel it, and most of SCRUB is SCRU
something tiny is insignificant in size

annotation.surface: Calling off most of an inquiry that hardly mattered anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scrub' for cancel is wartime RAF slang that stuck, as in a scrubbed sortie. 'Mostly' always takes the last letter, never the first.
annotation.definitionFit: Scrutiny is close searching examination, the kind of looking into a matter that an investigation means.

entries.clue: US city’s year satisfactory with Republican brought in after big city upset (3,4)

indicatorNotes.brought in: Someone brought in is fetched inside, so this letter goes among the ones already standing.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after a thing follows it, so in a down entry the earlier letters sit lower in the column.
indicatorNotes.upset: In a down clue something upset has been tipped over, so those letters are read upwards.

blocks.note: the Great Wen is Cobbett's old nickname for London, WEN tipped over
y = year, as in 5y
OK is satisfactory, and it opens to take the next letter
R is the letter beside a Republican's name on an American ballot

annotation.surface: A city's year going well once a Republican arrived, after trouble in a bigger one.
annotation.walkthrough: The Great Wen was William Cobbett's contemptuous name for London, a wen being a swelling on the skin. 'Big city' is doing duty twice: the one in the wordplay is not the one being defined.
annotation.definitionFit: New York is a city of the United States, the one most people mean by the phrase, so the definition simply states what it is.

entries.clue: Soccer team backed bringing in that chap, top man in hot surroundings? (4)

indicatorNotes.backed: A thing backed is turned to face the other way, so the club's two letters are written in reverse.
indicatorNotes.bringing in: Bringing someone in makes room for him inside, so this pair sits between the letters already there.

blocks.note: FC is the Football Club after every English team's name, here written backwards
that chap is he

annotation.surface: Punters backing a football team that has just signed a particular player.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backed' is the reversal and not the betting. FC is the tag on every club from Accrington Stanley upwards, and it is the only abbreviation in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A chef runs the kitchen, the hottest room in the building, so the definition describes the job rather than naming it.

entries.clue: French boyfriend engaged in surreptitious relations (6)

indicatorNotes.engaged in: To be engaged in something is to be caught up inside it, so these letters sit within the others.

blocks.note: fly is British slang for sly and knowing, as in a fly one
a Frenchwoman's boyfriend is her ami, the French for friend

annotation.surface: A French boyfriend caught up in a secret affair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fly' meaning sly is the British sense — a fly customer is one you cannot catch out. 'Relations' is the blood sense, not the affair the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Relations, in the plural, are the people you are related to — aunts, cousins, in-laws — which is a family.

entries.clue: Finished refrain in swamp (10)

blocks.note: when a thing is over it is finished
the burden of a song is its refrain, the line that comes round again

annotation.surface: The last chorus of a song dying away out on the marshes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Burden' for the refrain of a song is the old sense, kept alive by setters long after singers dropped it. 'Swamp' is the verb, to overwhelm, not the marsh the surface paints.
annotation.definitionFit: To overburden someone is to load them with more than they can carry, which is what swamping a person with work does.

entries.clue: Following Frenchmen in France he gets covered in earth with a sticky feel (8)

indicatorNotes.Following: What follows something comes along behind it, so the French word is written after the two Frenchmen.
indicatorNotes.gets covered in: Being covered in earth leaves it all round you, so those letters close over what they cover.

blocks.note: clay is earth, and it splits after its first three letters
MM is the French plural of M for Monsieur, used for two or more men
il is 'he' in French

annotation.surface: A man in France ending up caked in wet soil behind two other Frenchmen.
annotation.walkthrough: The French comes twice over: MM for a pair of Monsieurs, il for 'he'. The answer is an adverb, which is why the definition has to be a phrase starting 'with'.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done clammily is done with the cold damp stickiness of a nervous handshake, which is the sticky feel meant.

entries.clue: Hopeless, after Bishop released stuff not meant for release? (4)

indicatorNotes.released: Letting a thing go releases it, and a letter released from a word is simply gone from it.

blocks.note: a bleak outlook is a hopeless one
B is the bishop on a chess scoresheet

annotation.surface: A bishop, once let out, handing round papers nobody meant to publish.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the definition describes the thing rather than translating it — the material, not the act. B for bishop comes off the chessboard.
annotation.definitionFit: A leak is the confidential material that reaches the press by a back door, which is exactly what was never meant to be released.

entries.clue: Surprised comment about world leader yielding power in rebellion (6)

indicatorNotes.about: A remark made about someone goes round its subject, so these letters close over the name.
indicatorNotes.yielding: To yield a thing is to give it up, so that letter is surrendered and never written.

blocks.note: 'my!' is the surprised comment, and it parts to take the rest
Vladimir Putin, the Russian president
p = power, the letter given up

annotation.surface: An astonished remark about a head of state surrendering power during an uprising.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yielding power' is the joke: a president who gives up nothing but the letter p. 'My!' is a small exclamation setters lean on whenever they need those two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A mutiny is a rising by crew or soldiers against the officers over them, which is a rebellion.

entries.clue: Mark has excellent staff (4)

blocks.note: M was the mark, Germany's currency before the euro
ace means excellent, first-rate

annotation.surface: A man called Mark who employs first-rate people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like employees and is the pole: the one carried before the Speaker in the Commons, without which the House cannot sit. Mark is the German coin, not the name.
annotation.definitionFit: A mace is the ornamental staff carried before a mayor or a Speaker as the emblem of their authority.

entries.clue: Flower trouble kept returning (6)

indicatorNotes.returning: A thing returning comes back the way it went, so both pieces are written in reverse.

blocks.note: kept is HAD, coming back the other way
to trouble is to ail, and AIL turns round too

annotation.surface: Bother with the flowerbed that kept coming back year after year.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one continuous grumble, with nothing to mark where the wordplay starts; only the first word is the definition. Both little words turn together, which is why the instruction waits until the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A dahlia is a garden flower with a tight ball of petals, named after Dahl, the Swedish botanist.

entries.clue: Depth? Start to relish one board game involving knight (8)

indicatorNotes.Start to: Where a word starts is its opening letter, so only the first letter of what follows is taken.
indicatorNotes.involving: To involve someone is to draw them into the middle of the business, so these letters close round the next one.

blocks.note: the first letter of RELISH
the Roman numeral for one
chess is the board game, and it opens after its first two letters
N is the knight in chess notation, since K is taken by the king

annotation.surface: Starting to enjoy a board game in which a knight is causing trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: The knight is N because the king has already claimed K, a chess convention worth owning outright. The game in the wordplay is the same one the knight came from, which is how the surface holds together.
annotation.definitionFit: Richness is depth in the sense a flavour or a colour has it, the quality of having a great deal packed in.
